<reason>A genuinely close, high-quality debate. PRO kept the motion's natural reading in front of the judge: where the credential is stipulated not to drive performance, CON must defend keeping it anyway. PRO's first rebuttal landed two real hits—the tension between "nobody can know which screens are useless" and "competition punishes useless screens," and the reframe that work history is direct evidence of grit while the degree is only a proxy. PRO's pressure question on "degree or equivalent experience" forced CON into convergence, and PRO's antibiotics analogy neutralized CON's "who decides" trap by showing the motion is coherent advice to the decider. CON's late game was strong and original—the fixed-reading-capacity mechanism, the degree as the one connectionless credential, and "the only gate with a published price"—and PRO's closing ("adding doors doesn't shrink the building") did not fully engage that mechanism. But CON's own "hiring barely changed" claim undercut the scale of the harm, the transparency-loss residue was speculative, and CON was clipped twice. On balance PRO made the choice easier to decide and carried the cost asymmetry; a razor-thin edge to B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [B2.1]–[B2.3] exchange: exposing the contradiction between the unknowability claim and the market-correction claim, then turning CON's grit argument by showing a promoted warehouse lead has demonstrated the trait the degree only predicts—forcing CON into the "degree or equivalent experience" concession that PRO then exploited in Q1.</best_rebuttal>
